The salt spray stung Elias’s face as he hauled the last crate of oil up the spiral stairs. The lamp, a monstrous brass beast, was already lit, its beam cutting a pale, trembling path across the black Atlantic. He was sixty-one, and his hands knew the rhythm of the wicks better than his own heartbeat. The storm outside was a screaming, wet fury, but inside the lighthouse, it was just the hum of the flame and the groan of the stone.

He was about to settle into his chair, a worn leather thing that smelled of pipe smoke and old coffee, when he saw it. A small, damp envelope, sealed with a blob of red wax, resting on the cold iron of the lamp’s base. It hadn’t been there an hour ago. He hadn’t heard a knock, a footstep, or the creak of the door. He picked it up, feeling the slick, cold paper. The wax was cracked, and the seal was a strange, swirling symbol he didn’t recognize.

He opened it. The paper inside was thick, almost parchment-like, and the handwriting was a tight, elegant scrawl.
